Asparagus.about: Harvest established beds only; skip heavy cutting while young crowns establish.
signals: Spears are tender with tight, closed tips.
Plants are established and vigorous, not in their first growing season.
Stop when spears become thin and let ferns grow.
how: Cut or snap spears near ground level without damaging emerging spears.
Leave later growth to feed the crown.
after: Cool promptly and keep cut ends from drying.

Kale.about: Pick tender leaves as plants grow, keeping the growing center intact.
signals: Outer leaves are useful size and still tender.
The growing point is healthy and intact.
Avoid badly damaged or yellow leaves.
how: Pick lower outer leaves first.
Leave enough foliage for continued growth.
after: Wash just before preparing or dry well before storage.

Swiss Chard.about: Harvest outer leaves and stalks before they become coarse.
signals: Blades are expanded, crisp and not tough.
Petiole size suits the planned use.
Enough young leaves remain to continue growing.
how: Cut outer stalks near the base without injuring the crown.
Take modest amounts from small plants.

Cabbage.about: A full head should feel dense and firm before harvest.
signals: The head feels firm under gentle pressure.
It has reached the expected size for the cultivar.
how: Cut below the head with a clean knife.
Remove damaged outer leaves.
after: Keep only sound heads for longer storage.

Cauliflower.about: Cut heads while curds remain compact, before loosening or flowering.
signals: The head is tight and compact.
Individual flower structures are not spreading apart.
Color matches the cultivar, without browning.
how: Cut the head with a short stem and protective wrapper leaves.
Check frequently as maturity approaches.
after: Use soon for the best texture.

Brussels Sprouts.about: Pick firm sprouts from the lower stem upward as they mature.
signals: Lower sprouts feel firm and well formed.
Sprouts are tight, not loose or yellowing.
Upper sprouts can remain to enlarge.
how: Twist or cut individual sprouts from the stem.
Avoid damaging sprouts that will be picked later.
after: Trim damaged outer leaves before use.

Turnip.about: Young roots and greens are usually more tender than oversized plants.
signals: Root shoulders are near the cultivar's expected size.
A test root is crisp, not pithy or woody.
how: Loosen soil before pulling roots.
Cut greens above the crown if keeping the plant for more growth.

Parsnip.about: Dig mature roots after a cool growing season; soil must remain workable.
signals: A test root has useful diameter and length.
The cultivar's long growing period has elapsed.
Soil can be worked without breaking roots.
how: Loosen soil deeply beside the row.
Handle foliage carefully
sap can irritate skin in sunlight.
after: Use gloves and avoid skin contact with sap.

Eggplant.about: Harvest glossy, firm fruit before seeds harden and skin becomes dull.
signals: The surface is glossy for the variety.
Fruit is firm with slight give.
A sample fruit has soft, pale seeds rather than hard brown ones.
how: Cut with pruners, leaving a short stem.
Watch for prickles on stems and calyx.

Okra.about: Small tender pods are preferable; pods become fibrous quickly.
signals: Pods are young and near the cultivar's tender picking size.
Pods are tender rather than woody.
New pods are checked often during hot weather.
how: Snip pods with a short stem.
Wear gloves if stems irritate your skin.
after: Remove tough oversized pods so picking remains manageable.

Winter Squash.about: Harvest fully mature fruit before a damaging freeze.
signals: The rind is hard and resists a light thumbnail impression.
The stem is becoming corky and dry.
Skin color matches mature fruit for the cultivar.
how: Cut with a length of stem attached.
Handle by the fruit, not the stem.
after: Cure only varieties suited to curing.
Store sound fruit cool and dry, following cultivar guidance.

Pumpkin.about: Select fully colored, hard-rinded fruit before severe frost.
signals: The fruit has developed mature cultivar color.
The stem is drying and firm.
how: Cut with a sturdy stem handle attached.
Do not carry fruit by the stem.
after: Keep dry and protect from freezing.
Check stored fruit for soft spots.

Sweet Potato.about: Harvest after roots size up and before cold soil or frost damages them.
signals: A test dig shows useful storage-root size.
Harvest is planned before frost and chilling.
Roots are handled gently because fresh skins bruise easily.
how: Loosen soil well outside the crown.
Lift without cutting or throwing roots.
after: Cure in warm, humid, ventilated conditions using Extension guidance.
do not treat them like white potatoes.

Sweet Corn.about: Eat sweet corn soon after picking for the best quality.
signals: The ear feels filled to the tip.
A test kernel releases milky liquid, not clear liquid or thick dough.
how: Hold the stalk and twist the ear downward.
Check a sample rather than relying on silk color alone.
after: Use as soon as practical after picking.

Peas.about: Harvest stage depends on whether you grow shelling, snap or snow peas.
signals: Pods remain tender and fresh green.
Peas have not turned hard or starchy.
how: Hold the vine while picking.
Harvest frequently as pods mature.
after: Use quickly for the best sweetness.

Dry Beans.about: Dry beans mature later than snap beans and need dry seed storage.
signals: Beans are hard and fully colored.
Bring pods under cover if prolonged rain threatens.
how: Pick dry pods or pull mature plants for sheltered drying.
Keep batches labeled by variety.
after: Dry thoroughly before sealing in containers.

Fava Beans.about: For fresh eating, pick filled pods while beans are still tender.
signals: Pods are well filled and green.
A sample bean is full-sized but not hard or mealy.
Pods have not dried down unless saving dry seed.
how: Support the stem while picking.
Use snips if pods do not detach easily.
after: People with G6PD deficiency should follow their clinician's advice about fava beans.

Leek.about: Leeks can be lifted when their blanched shanks reach a useful size.
signals: The white stem is the desired thickness.
Soil is workable for lifting without tearing roots.
how: Loosen soil with a fork beside the row.
Lift instead of pulling hard.

Green Onion.about: Harvest slender immature onions for tender leaves and stems.
signals: Stems have reached the thickness needed for use.
A large storage bulb is not required.
how: Loosen soil before lifting whole plants.
Take a few at a time for fresh use.
after: Trim damaged tips and wash before preparing.

Raspberry.about: Pick fully colored berries that release easily from the receptacle.
signals: Fruit matches mature color for the cultivar.
The berry slips off with a gentle pull.
Berries are soft but intact, not leaking.
how: Use shallow containers.
Pick frequently and keep fruit shaded.

Blueberry.about: Blue color alone may precede the sweetest picking stage.
signals: The entire berry is blue without a red stem end.
A ripe berry rolls gently from the cluster.
A sample is sweet enough for the intended use.
how: Roll ripe berries into your hand without squeezing.
Leave tight, tart berries to finish.
after: Keep berries dry until washing before use.

Blackberry.about: Pick glossy-to-dull black berries only when they release readily.
signals: Fruit is fully black for the cultivar.
A sample has ripe flavor rather than strong tartness.
how: Handle gently and use shallow containers.
Wear protection near thorny canes.

Apple.about: Ripeness depends strongly on cultivar and intended storage.
signals: Background color changes as expected for the cultivar.
A sample has developed the expected flavor and texture.
Fruit detaches with a gentle lift and twist.
how: Lift and twist without pulling spur wood.
Keep bruised fruit separate.
after: seed color alone is not a reliable maturity test.

Grape.about: Grapes do not become sweeter after picking; sample before cutting.
signals: Berries from different parts of the bunch taste mature.
Berries are filled and not shriveled.
how: Snip bunches from the vine.
Handle bunches without squeezing berries.

Cilantro.about: Pick leafy stems before bolting for leaf use; mature seed is coriander.
signals: There is enough fresh leafy growth to cut lightly.
Heavy flowering signals declining leaf production.
how: Snip outer stems while leaving young growth.
Sow small successive batches for continued leaves.
after: For coriander, dry mature seed heads separately.

Dill.about: Leaf, flower-head and seed harvests happen at different stages.
signals: Feathery foliage is fresh and aromatic.
Flowering heads suit pickling before seeds harden.
Seed heads turn brown for dry spice harvest.
how: Snip leaves lightly without stripping young plants.
Collect seed heads into a bag before seeds scatter.

Parsley.about: Take outer stems so the center can continue growing.
signals: Outer leaves are full-sized and fresh.
how: Cut outer stems near the base.
Leave the center growing point intact.

Lavender.about: Cut flowering stems at a stage suited to fresh use or drying.
signals: For drying, many growers cut when lower florets begin opening.
Spikes are dry, fresh and free from browning.
Enough leafy growth remains below the cut.
how: Cut above the woody base without stripping the plant.
Gather small bundles after dew dries.
after: Dry with airflow out of direct sun.
Use only known culinary lavender grown for edible use if cooking with it.
